introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2026. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry TWENTY-FIVE marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

figures.legende: Schematic fall of economic rent with distance from the city for three land uses, with the margin of cultivation where the rent reaches zero (model answer to Q5(a)(i)).

incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section » (Section A : questions 1 à 3, Section B : questions 4 à 6, Section C : question 7 seule). `regles_choix` porte le minimum imposé par section (`parmi 1 sur 3` pour A et B, `parmi 1 sur 1` pour C) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. La question 7 offre deux versions (EITHER / OR) : sous-questions codées « a », « b » (EITHER) et « OR-a », « OR-b » (OR), reliées par une règle `ou` (deux sous-questions « a » dans un même exercice seraient refusées).

Question 5(a)(ii) : le sujet laisse le choix entre deux questions (EITHER industries « foot loose » / OR couloirs maritimes), chacune de 7 marks, à l'intérieur de la sous-question « a » (16 points : (i) 9 + (ii) 7). La règle `ou` s'applique à tout un groupe de sections et ne peut donc pas l'exprimer sans fausser les questions 4 et 6 ; le corrigé traite les deux versions de (ii), signalées « EITHER » et « OR (alternative question) ».

Points : chaque question est imprimée à 25 marks et les sous-parties somment bien à 25 (Q1 6+4+4+6+5 ; Q2 8+8+9 ; Q3 8+9+8 ; Q4 9+9+7 ; Q5 9+7+9 ; Q6 4+6+6+9 ; Q7 EITHER 15+10, OR 5+5+9+6). Les sous-questions regroupant des parties (i) et (ii) (1a, 1b, 5a, 6a, OR-a, OR-b) portent la somme de leurs marks (10, 10, 16, 10, 10, 15) ; les marks de chaque partie restent imprimés dans l'énoncé. Aucun écart avec le sujet.

Défauts d'impression du sujet, transcrits avec le minimum de retouches : Q1(a) « heavy or less precipitation » (formulation maladroite, recopiée) ; Q2(a) se termine par deux points (« surface.. »), un seul conservé ; Q4 « The unven distribution » (faute d'impression pour « uneven », corrigée dans la transcription) ; Q4(c) se termine par une virgule (« sparsely populated, ») ; Q5(a)(ii) une apostrophe parasite devant « Discuss » (non recopiée) ; Q5(a)(ii) OR et Q5(b) se terminent par un point d'interrogation alors que la phrase est une consigne (« Explain... ? », « Explain THREE efforts... sector? »), recopié tel quel ; Q7 la version OR n'est pas numérotée (« OR » puis a), b)) et les parties (i) et (ii) du b) de la version OR sont numérotées « i) » et « ii) » sous « b) ». La page 3 du scan montre en marge gauche des fragments de caractères sans lien avec le sujet, ignorés.

Sujet scanné de trois pages (page de garde, deux pages de questions), filigranes et bandeaux gcerevision.com sans incidence sur la lecture, ignorés. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Geography 2, Paper 2, code 0750, JUNE 2026, THREE HOURS, référence GCE26/0750/2/P52. Aucune carte, aucun graphique ni document imprimé dans ce sujet : aucune figure d'énoncé ; les trois figures déclarées (profil de sol, courbes de Malthus et de Boserup, rente économique de Von Thünen) sont des schémas qualitatifs produits pour les corrigés (origine « corrige »), non à l'échelle, sans valeur numérique.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les exemples cités (lieux, programmes, accords, institutions) sont des exemples reconnus ; les chiffres sont des ordres de grandeur donnés avec « about », « roughly » ou « more than ». Les faits cités sont à faire relire par un géographe avant toute mise en avant.

Question 1(c) : la description de la pluviométrie de la zone équatoriale du Cameroun (type guinéen à quatre saisons de 1500 à 2000 mm environ, type camerounais côtier de plus de 3000 mm, Debundscha à plus de 9000 mm certaines années) reprend les chiffres courants des manuels, donnés comme ordres de grandeur ; limites de la zone « au sud de 6 degrés nord environ » approximatives. Question 1(b)(ii) : barrage de Lagdo « construit au début des années 1980 » et Q7(b) barrage de Maga, SEMRY, « Opération Sahel Vert lancée à la fin des années 1980 » : dates approximatives à vérifier.

Question 2(c) : les altitudes (basses terres côtières « en dessous de 200 m environ », basses terres du Nord « 200 à 500 m environ », lac Tchad « environ 280 m », mont Cameroun « environ 4000 m ») sont des ordres de grandeur ; la nature de la ligne volcanique du Cameroun (point chaud ou ligne de faiblesse) est présentée comme débattue. Question 2(b) : l'exemple de Keta (Ghana) et l'érosion de la côte camerounaise sont cités sans détail. Question 2(a) : dates de Wegener (1912, 1915) et de Pangée (« il y a environ 200 millions d'années ») sont des repères courants.

Question 4(c) : les bassins de Ndian et de Mamfe sont décrits d'après les manuels camerounais (forêt dense, marécages et inondations, maladies, isolement, parc national de Korup) ; aucun chiffre de densité n'est donné. Le point sur l'insécurité récente (régions du Sud-Ouest et du Nord-Ouest) est un fait contemporain cité avec prudence.

Question 5(b) : les actions de l'État cité (barrage de Lom Pangar, Memve'ele, centrale à gaz de Kribi, projet de Nachtigal, port en eau profonde de Kribi, régime des zones franches depuis le début des années 1990, Charte des investissements de 2002, Cameroon Business Forum, stratégies DSCE et SND 2020-2030) sont des faits reconnus mais l'état d'avancement actuel de chaque projet (en particulier Nachtigal) et les dates exactes sont à vérifier. Question 6(c) : taux d'urbanisation « d'environ 55 à 60 pour cent » = estimation récente, ordre de grandeur.

Question 7(a) : exemples cités (crues de printemps de la Red River en 1997, tsunami de décembre 2004 avec plus de 200 000 morts, tsunami du Tohoku en 2011, crues du Yangtsé en 1998 en partie attribuées à la déforestation, inondations de Douala et de Yaoundé) reconnus mais à faire relire ; le rôle de la déforestation dans les crues du Yangtsé reste discuté.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) i) Explain THREE reasons for the decrease in the Economic Rent of a farmer with distance from the city.

(9 marks)

ii) *EITHER* Discuss THREE reasons why present-day industries are becoming foot loose in nature.

*OR*

Explain why most shipping routes follow specific lanes or water paths despite the fact that the world's oceans form a continuous expanse of water linking the continents?

(7 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Reasons for the decrease in economic rent with distance (9 marks)**

**Economic rent** (the concept of Von Thunen's agricultural location model) is the **profit** a farmer makes on a unit of land: the value of the crop at the market, **minus the cost of production, minus the cost of transport** to the market in the city. It is highest on the land next to the city and falls as the distance increases, until it reaches zero at the **margin of cultivation**, where it is no longer worth growing that crop.

![fig-1](gce-al-geography-2026-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_5_fig_1.png)

1. **Transport costs rise with distance.** The transport cost is proportional to the distance (more fuel, time and labour per tonne), while the price received at the market is the same wherever the crop was grown. The farther the farm is from the city, the larger the share of the price taken by transport and the smaller the profit. Von Thunen's relation can be written: rent = (price - production cost) x yield - (yield x transport rate x distance).
2. **Perishable and bulky products lose value or are lost on the way.** Crops that spoil quickly (vegetables, milk, fruit) or are heavy and bulky (firewood) cannot be sent far: they spoil, lose weight or quality, or need costly fast and refrigerated transport. Fewer of them reach the market, so their rent falls steeply with distance, and they are grown close to the city, while durable and low-bulk products (grain, livestock) can be grown farther out.
3. **Intensity of production and yield fall with distance.** The farmer far from the city can use less capital, labour and fertiliser (inputs bought or hired in the city are dearer and less available), so the **yield per hectare falls** and the system changes from intensive to **extensive** (market gardening and dairying near the city; cereals, then ranching and grazing farther out). Lower output per hectare means a smaller rent.
4. **Land value and competition for land fall.** Near the city, many users compete for the land, so the land is valuable and the rent is high; far from the city the demand for the land falls, and so does the rent.
5. **Reduced access to market information, credit, storage and services** increases the farmer's costs and risks.

(Any three reasons, clearly explained, earn full marks.)

**(ii) EITHER: reasons why industries are becoming foot loose (7 marks)**

A **foot-loose industry** is one that is **not tied to a particular location** by the need to be near raw materials, power or markets: it can locate in many places. Three reasons (about 2 to 3 marks each):

1. **Light, high-value, low-bulk products and components.** Industries such as electronics, computers, pharmaceuticals, software and jewellery use small amounts of light, valuable materials and produce goods that are cheap to carry compared with their value, so **transport costs are a minor part of the total costs** and they do not need to be near the raw material or the market.
2. **Improved transport and communications and the widespread availability of power.** Motorways, container ships, air freight, the Internet and mobile telephones allow the parts and the finished products to be moved quickly and cheaply and the production to be controlled from far away; **electricity from the national grid** (rather than coal fields or waterfalls) and gas pipelines mean that factories do not have to be near the energy source.
3. **Other factors become more important than the resource: skilled labour, government incentives, the environment and the market.** Firms choose places with a **skilled and cheap labour force**, **science parks and universities** (research and development), **tax incentives and free zones**, a pleasant environment and good infrastructure for their managers (Silicon Valley, the Cambridge Science Park; assembly plants in the free zones of Asia). **Globalisation and transnational companies** can split the production process among countries and move it in search of lower costs.
4. (Also) the growth of **service and high-technology industries** and of **small-scale firms**, which can work from small premises.

**OR: why shipping routes follow specific lanes (7 marks)** (alternative question)

Although the oceans are continuous, ships do not sail across them at random, because:

1. **The shortest route is the cheapest.** Ships follow **great-circle routes** (the shortest distance between two ports) and the routes that link the **main ports and trading regions** (North America, Europe, East Asia), so that the traffic is concentrated on a few busy lanes such as the North Atlantic and the Europe-Asia route.
2. **Natural and artificial passages and straits.** Ships must pass through **narrow, deep and safe channels**: the Suez and Panama canals, the Strait of Malacca, the Strait of Gibraltar and the Strait of Hormuz, or round the Cape of Good Hope. They are **choke points** that save thousands of kilometres.
3. **Safety and the natural conditions.** Ships avoid areas with **icebergs, pack ice, reefs, shallow waters, storms and hurricanes**, and use the **ocean currents and winds** (they follow favourable currents and avoid contrary ones) to save fuel; **traffic-separation schemes** in busy waters reduce collisions.
4. **Ports and bunkering stations.** The routes link the **deep-water ports** with the necessary equipment, and the ships call at fuelling and supply points; the **hinterlands** of the ports and the volume of trade decide the busiest routes.
5. **International regulations and security** (the rules of the International Maritime Organization, piracy zones to be avoided or protected).

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) Explain THREE efforts made by the government of Cameroon to solve the problems plaguing the industrial sector?

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The problems of the industrial sector** in Cameroon include an insufficient and unreliable supply of **electricity**, poor **transport infrastructure** and high transport costs, a lack of **capital** and of credit, a **narrow home market**, **competition** from cheap imports and smuggling, a shortage of skilled labour, heavy **taxes and bureaucracy**, and a weak private sector. The government has made the following efforts (three well explained, 3 marks each).

1. **Increasing the supply of energy.** The government has invested, often with foreign partners, in power plants and dams to meet the demand of industry: the **Lom Pangar** reservoir dam (which regulates the flow of the Sanaga and increases the output of the Song Loulou and Edea power stations), the **Memve'ele** hydroelectric dam, the **Kribi gas power plant** and the **Nachtigal** hydropower project. Electricity from the national grid is also extended to industrial zones. The aim is to cut power failures and costs.
2. **Improving infrastructure and creating industrial zones and free zones.** The government builds and rehabilitates roads and railways, and has developed the **deep-sea port of Kribi** and its industrial complex (to attract metal, wood-processing and agro-industrial plants and to reduce the congestion of Douala port); it has created **industrial zones** (Douala-Bonaberi, Bassa and others) and the **free zone regime** (since the early 1990s), in which export firms are exempt from many taxes and duties and are given facilities.
3. **Incentives, a better business climate and support to small firms.** Successive **investment codes and incentive laws** (the Investment Charter of 2002 and the later laws on incentives for private investment) give **tax and customs benefits** to approved firms; the government has simplified procedures for creating firms (one-stop centres), organised dialogue with business (the Cameroon Business Forum), and created support bodies and credit schemes for **small and medium-sized enterprises**. Since the 1990s, the **privatisation** of loss-making state companies was also meant to make them more efficient.
4. (Other acceptable efforts) **industrial development plans** (the industrialisation strategy of the Growth and Employment Strategy Paper and the National Development Strategy 2020-2030), the training of technicians and engineers in technical schools and universities, the fight against smuggling and counterfeit goods, the policy of **import substitution** and of **processing local raw materials** (cocoa, timber, cotton), and regional integration (CEMAC and the African Continental Free Trade Area) to widen the market.

**Note.** A good answer also shows the limits of these efforts: electricity is still not fully reliable, many roads are poor, and the sector remains small compared with agriculture and services.
